Unit 6 check

About 20 minutes: one fresh question for each part of every outcome of Unit 6, plus two from earlier units to keep them sharp. It is not graded and only you see it.

An outcome becomes Secure when you have answered a question on each of its parts right first time, without a hint or the solution, here in this check. When all 4 are secure you are ready to try Canvas Quiz 6 (due Sun 22 Nov). Already know this material? Take the check before the lessons and skip what is secure.

ChooseRead r: direction, strength, straight lines only6b

Which scatter plot has a correlation closest to r=0.6r = 0.6r=0.6?

Plot A
The points rise from left to right with a clear trend, but with a lot of scatter around a line: a moderate association.
Plot B
The points fall from left to right with a clear trend, but with a lot of scatter around a line: a moderate association. Its r is about −0.6, not close to 0.6.
Plot C
The points rise from left to right and lie close to a straight line: a strong positive linear association. Its r is about 0.95, not close to 0.6.
Plot D
The points fall from left to right and lie close to a straight line: a strong negative linear association. Its r is about −0.95, not close to 0.6.
ChooseCorrelation is not causation6b

Countries that eat more chocolate per person win more Nobel prizes per person. Which conclusion is justified?

Chocolate eaten and Nobel prizes won go together, but this does not show that one causes the other
The data show an association. A third variable, national wealth, could explain it.
Eating chocolate helps people win Nobel prizes
An association alone does not show a cause. Here national wealth is a likely explanation of both.
Winning Nobel prizes makes a country eat more chocolate
An association alone does not show a cause; here national wealth is a likely explanation of both.
There is no real link between chocolate eaten and Nobel prizes won: correlation is not causation
The association is real: the data show it. What they do not show is why.

ChooseInterpret slope and intercept6c

Your answerUpdate each centre to the mean of its points6d

After an assignment, cluster 2 holds the points (−1,−1)(-1, -1)(−1,−1), (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3), (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5), (−2,3)(-2, 3)(−2,3). Its old centre was (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3). In the update, where does c2\mathbf{c}_2c2​ move? Give its first coordinate, to 2 decimal places if needed.

You averaged in the old centre as well. The new centre is the mean of the cluster's points only.
That is the median. k-means moves each centre to the mean.
That is the sum. Divide by the number of points, 4.
That is the mean of the second coordinates.
The new centre is the mean of the cluster's points, one coordinate at a time. The old centre plays no part.
Solution

((−1)+2+0+(−2))/4=−0.25((-1) + 2 + 0 + (-2))/4 = -0.25((−1)+2+0+(−2))/4=−0.25.

Review: Unit 6 · Lesson 6.4 · Assign, update, repeat

ChooseWhy and how to standardise before clustering6d

You cluster penguins on body mass (g, SD 800) and bill depth (mm, SD 2), without standardising. What decides the clusters?

Almost only the body mass
A typical body mass difference (800 g) is a far larger number than a typical bill depth difference (2 mm), so it swamps the squared distances. Standardise both columns first.
Almost only the bill depth
k-means adds squared differences in each column's own units, and the bill depth differences are the small numbers.
Both equally, because the distance adds every column
Every column is added, but in its own units: the larger numbers dominate.
Neither: k-means ignores the units of the columns
The units are exactly what the distance sees: a difference of 1 g counts the same as 1 mm.

Keeping sharp (earlier units — not counted)

ChooseCorrelation is not causation6b

People who use a walking stick walk more slowly than people who do not. Which is the most likely explanation?

The cause runs the other way: people who walk slowly or unsteadily are the ones given walking sticks
The walking slowly comes first and leads to the using a walking stick, not the reverse.
A third variable, shoe size, affects both using a walking stick and walking slowly
There is no reason to think shoe size affects either; the link runs the other way.
Using a walking stick makes people walk more slowly
That reads the association as a cause, in one particular direction. Here it most likely runs the other way.
It is pure coincidence: the two have nothing to do with each other
The link is too consistent, and too easy to explain, to be pure chance.

Review: Unit 6 · Lesson 6.3 · Slope and intercept by formula

Interpret slope and intercept

Taught in Lesson 6.3 · The least-squares line.

Choose6c

For 195 adults, with hours of exercise per week from 0 to 12 hours, a least-squares line predicts the resting heart rate yyy (bpm) from the hours of exercise per week xxx (hours): y^=−1.2x+70\hat{y} = -1.2x + 70y^​=−1.2x+70. What does the intercept, 70, tell you?

The predicted resting heart rate for a adult with hours of exercise per week 0 hours, 70 bpm
The intercept is the line's value at x=0x = 0x=0, and hours of exercise per week 0 hours is inside the data (0 to 12 hours), so it is a real prediction.
The smallest resting heart rate in the data
The intercept is the line's value at x=0x = 0x=0, not the smallest observed value.
How much the predicted resting heart rate changes for each extra 1 hour of hours of exercise per week
That is the slope, −1.2.
The predicted resting heart rate at hours of exercise per week 0 hours, 70 bpm: an extrapolation far outside the data (0 to 12 hours), with no real meaning
Here hours of exercise per week 0 hours lies inside the data (0 to 12 hours), so it is not an extrapolation.
Choose6c

For 190 students, with hours of revision from 0 to 20 hours, a least-squares line predicts the exam mark yyy (marks) from the hours of revision xxx (hours): y^=2.8x+41\hat{y} = 2.8x + 41y^​=2.8x+41. What does the slope, 2.8, tell you?

Students with 1 hour more hours of revision have a predicted exam mark about 2.8 marks higher, on average
The slope is the change in predicted yyy for each extra 1 hour of xxx: 2.8 marks per hour, a difference between students.
Students with 1 hour more hours of revision have a predicted exam mark about 2.8 marks lower, on average
Check the sign: the slope 2.8 is positive.
The exam mark goes up by 2.8% for each extra 1 hour
The slope is in the units of yyy per unit of xxx (marks per hour), not a percentage.
A student with hours of revision 1 hour has a predicted exam mark of 2.8 marks
That leaves out the intercept: at x=1x = 1x=1 the line gives 2.8+41=43.82.8 + 41 = 43.82.8+41=43.8.

The predicted price at floor area 0 m², £40 thousand: an extrapolation far outside the data (30 to 120 m²), with no real meaning
The intercept is the line's value at x=0x = 0x=0. No flat in the data comes near floor area 0, so it only anchors the line.
The smallest price in the data
The intercept is the line's value at x=0x = 0x=0, not the smallest observed value.
The average price of the flats
The average is yˉ\bar{y}yˉ​. The line passes through (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar{x}, \bar{y})(xˉ,yˉ​), not through (0,yˉ)(0, \bar{y})(0,yˉ​).
How much the predicted price changes for each extra 1 m² of floor area
That is the slope, 3.3.

Compute and interpret r²

Taught in Lesson 6.3 · The least-squares line.

Choose6c

A least-squares line predicting the body mass of penguins from their flipper length has r2=0.74r^2 = 0.74r2=0.74. Which statement is right?

About 74% of the variation in body mass is accounted for by the line on flipper length
r2=1−∑ei2/∑(yi−yˉ)2r^2 = 1 - \sum e_i^2 / \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2r2=1−∑ei2​/∑(yi​−yˉ​)2: the residuals leave about 26% of the variation, so the line accounts for 74%.
About 74% of the penguins lie on the line
r2r^2r2 compares sums of squares; it does not count points on the line.
The flipper length causes 74% of the body mass
r2r^2r2 describes an association in these data, not a cause.
About 86% of the variation in body mass is accounted for by the line on flipper length
That is r=0.74r = \sqrt{0.74}r=0.74​ as a percentage. The proportion is r2r^2r2 itself.
Your answer6c

A least-squares line predicting the exam mark of students from their hours of revision has a negative slope and r2=0.64r^2 = 0.64r2=0.64. What is Pearson's r?

That is r2r^2r2. Take its square root to get the size of r.
The slope is negative, so r is negative too: they always share a sign.
r2r^2r2 is the square of r, so ∣r∣=r2|r| = \sqrt{r^2}∣r∣=r2​.
r has the same sign as the slope.
Solution

0.64=0.8\sqrt{0.64} = 0.80.64​=0.8, and the slope is negative, so r=−0.8r = -0.8r=−0.8.

That is the share left over in the residuals. Subtract it from 1.
Upside down: divide ∑ei2\sum e_i^2∑ei2​ by ∑(yi−yˉ)2\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2∑(yi​−yˉ​)2, then subtract from 1.

That is r as a percentage. Square it first: r2r^2r2.
That is r2r^2r2 as a proportion. The question asks for a percentage.
r2r^2r2 is a square, so it is never negative.
For a straight line with an intercept, the proportion of the variation accounted for is r2r^2r2.

Choose6d

To save time, you compare squared distances d2d^2d2 and skip the square root. Does any point change cluster?

No: for distances, which are never negative, d1<d2d_1 < d_2d1​<d2​ exactly when d12<d22d_1^2 < d_2^2d12​<d22​
Squaring keeps the order of numbers that are not negative, so the nearest centre stays the nearest.
Yes: squaring stretches large distances, so points far from every centre move
Squaring stretches the numbers but keeps their order.
Only when the columns are in different units
Units change the distances themselves, not whether you take the root. The order is the same either way.
Yes: every point moves to the centre that is furthest away
The smallest distance still has the smallest square.

What does this program print?

import numpy as np

# distances: one row per student, one column per centre
D = np.array([[7, 6],
              [2, 8],
              [5, 3],
              [4, 9],
              [8, 1]])
print(D.argmin(axis=1))
[1 0 1 0 1]
Along each row, the position (from 0) of its smallest distance: the nearest centre of each student.
[1 4]
That is axis=0: down each column, the nearest student to each centre.
[2 1 2 1 2]
NumPy counts positions from 0: the first column is 0.
[0 1 0 1 0]
That picks the largest distance in each row, as argmax would.

import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 7], [3, 4], [3, 5], [9, 4], [4, 4]])
c1 = np.array([2, 7])
c2 = np.array([8, 1])
c3 = np.array([7, 3])
d1 = np.sqrt(((X - c1) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
d2 = np.sqrt(((X - c2) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
d3 = np.sqrt(((X - c3) ** 2).sum(axis=1))

That is the row farthest from p (argmax).
3.16
That is the smallest distance itself. argmin gives where it is: a row index.
Choose6d

What does this program print?

import numpy as np

# distances: one row per house, one column per centre
D = np.array([[5, 2],
              [2, 5],
              [7, 9],
              [3, 6]])
print(D.argmin(axis=1))
[1 0 0 0]
Along each row, the position (from 0) of its smallest distance: the nearest centre of each house.
[1 0]
That is axis=0: down each column, the nearest house to each centre.
[2 1 1 1]
NumPy counts positions from 0: the first column is 0.
[0 1 1 1]
That picks the largest distance in each row, as argmax would.
Choose6d

What does this program print?

import numpy as np

X = np.array([[6, 5], [5, 1], [2, 1], [8, 4], [8, 3]])
c1 = np.array([6, 2])
c2 = np.array([8, 5])
d1 = np.sqrt(((X - c1) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
d2 = np.sqrt(((X - c2) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
labels = np.column_stack([d1, d2]).argmin(axis=1)
print(labels)
[1 0 0 1 1]
Each row of X gets the position (0 = c1) of its nearest centre, using both coordinates.
[2 1 1 2 2]
Positions count from 0: c1 is 0.
[0 0 0 1 1]
That compares the first coordinates only. The distances use both columns.
[0 1 1 0 0]
That is the farthest centre of each point.

k-means on penguins uses body mass and bill depth.

penguinbody mass (g)bill depth (mm)x436018.4c1340017.5c2348014.9\begin{array}{c|cc} \text{penguin} & \text{body mass (g)} & \text{bill depth (mm)} \\ \hline \mathbf{x} & 4360 & 18.4 \\ \mathbf{c}_1 & 3400 & 17.5 \\ \mathbf{c}_2 & 3480 & 14.9 \end{array}penguinxc1​c2​​body mass (g)436034003480​bill depth (mm)18.417.514.9​​

The SDs are 800 g for body mass and 2 mm for bill depth. Work out d(x,c2)d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}_2)d(x,c2​) in z-score units (each difference divided by its SD). Give 2 decimal places.

That is the distance in raw units. Divide each difference by its SD first.
That uses only the body mass. Include the standardised bill depth difference too.
That is the squared distance. Take its square root.
Divide each difference by its SD: body mass by 800, bill depth by 2.
Then square, add and take the square root.

(1.10)2+(1.75)2≈2.07\sqrt{(1.10)^2 + (1.75)^2} \approx 2.07(1.10)2+(1.75)2​≈2.07.

Cluster 2
In z-score units, d(x,c2)=(−0.60)2+(1.00)2≈1.17d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}_2) = \sqrt{(-0.60)^2 + (1.00)^2} \approx 1.17d(x,c2​)=(−0.60)2+(1.00)2​≈1.17, the smaller: after standardising, both columns count.
Cluster 1
In z-score units, d(x,c1)=(−0.10)2+(2.00)2≈2.00d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}_1) = \sqrt{(-0.10)^2 + (2.00)^2} \approx 2.00d(x,c1​)=(−0.10)2+(2.00)2​≈2.00. It is nearer only in raw units (4.5 against 24.0), where the floor area swamps the number of bedrooms.
Neither: it is equally far from both centres

Standardising cannot change which cluster a point joins

Divide each difference by its column's SD, then work out the distance.
